newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli Treasury, central bank at odds over budget.
newsitem.headline: Israeli Treasury, central bank at odds over budget.

text.p: Israel's Treasury and central bank could be on a collision course over the need for further budget cuts after the release of first-quarter budget figures on Wednesday, economists said.

The Treasury released preliminary spending data showing a first-quarter deficit of 1.37 billion shekels. The deficit has shown a steady improvement from month to month, with March registering a 188 million shekel surplus compared with a deficit of 1.0 billion in March last year. But the Treasury declined to say how far above target the quarterly deficit was.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel has been pushing hard for the Treasury to make cuts immediately to keep the deficit within the budgetary target of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product.

Pessimists among analysts say the government will miss that target by 0.8 percent of GDP, or three to four billion shekels. Improvements in comparison with 1996 should be ignored because last year's deficit was particularly bad.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor said he would review spending only at the end of the first quarter. On Wednesday he declined to comment on how the Treasury would act.

"I can only say after we've analysed them (the figures) and then we'll decide if there is a need for a budget cut and if so, how much and how we'll go about it," he said after the release of the figures.
Frenkel warned earlier in the week failure to reduce the deficit would exacerbate the slowdown and endanger Israel's credit rating.

"When it says it's going to try to reach its targets as far as the budget is concerned I take it seriously," he said. "Of course if we don't see that effort realised there will be room for concern because there will be basically two issues: one, a loss of credibility and second, a loss for the economy."
Economists are as divided as policymakers -- not only about how to act but if there is a problem at all.
Shauli Katznelson, chief economist at Israel Discount Bank, warned that the deficit is running dangerously ahead of forecasts.

"No one takes into account the issue of seasonality. You can't look at 1996, because the deficit was so big. But if you look at earlier years -- 1993, 1994 and 1995 -- you see in the first few months, up through May, there was almost no deficit, even a surplus," he said.
He said Discount was predicting the government would overshoot its deficit target by three billion to four billion shekels, equal to an additional 0.8 percent to one percent of GDP.
But Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, said the first-quarter figure was inflated by one-time payments of about one billion shekels to the quasi-public health care system.

"My present forecast is that they'll overshoot their target by 0.5 percent for 1997, or 1.5 to 1.6 billion shekels," Katz said. "That's no big deal if you compare it with 1996. A deficit of about three percent is not inflationary."

Katz said tax revenues had lagged early in the year but were starting to catch up with forecasts. He added that the government had been excessively bearish about inflation when it fixed the 1997 budget and therefore spending might come out under forecast.

But Katznelson warned that the budget was based on overly optimistic forecasts about how quickly the economy would expand this year. The budget assumes 4.0 percent growth, but Discount sees the economy expanding by no more than 2.5 percent to three percent.
